$about: The single source of truth for both toolkits' visual design (#345).
Desktop is Avalonia and mobile is Flutter; they share no styling primitive, so a brand
maintained by hand is two sources of truth that drift on the first change.
Generated artifacts (do not hand-edit -- CI fails on drift):
src/Aer.Ui/Theme/GeneratedTokens.axaml  Avalonia ThemeVariant resources
src/Aer.Mobile/lib/theme/tokens.dart  Flutter ThemeData
Regenerate with: pixi run tokens
Values are decision 0006's 'Quiet' direction, taken verbatim from the component gallery the
owner reviewed and chose -- not re-derived. Two rules from 0006 are structural here and must
survive a re-brand: semantic status colour is a ramp SEPARATE from the brand accent, and every
status carries a glyph and a word so it never depends on hue alone.

brand.$about: The accent. Changing these must not move anything under 'status'.

$about: Grounds and rules. 'sunk' is the recessed fill for selected rows and pills.
'code' is deliberately its own surface rather than a reuse of 'sunk'. Code has to read as
distinctly not-prose, and the honest lever for that is the surface it sits on, not a larger
type size: scaling code up overflows a phone's width and forces horizontal scrolling, which is
worse than the problem it solves. So code keeps the body size and gets its own ground.
The rule is directional, not a fixed elevation: code steps AWAY from the page ground, whichever
way stays comfortable -- down in light, up in dark. Going darker still in dark mode was the
obvious first instinct (an inset terminal) and was rejected on 0006's own reasoning: it rejected
the Signal direction partly because a near-black dark mode 'can feel harsh on OLED at night',
and a near-black code panel imports that harshness back onto the surface stared at longest.
The block carries a border and a header, so it does not need near-black to read as its own
object.
'codeInline' is a second, much quieter treatment, and the split is not fussiness. A block owns
its own rectangle and can afford a strong ground; an inline span sits inside a running line, so
the same strength would shred the paragraph it lives in. Inline therefore lifts slightly in dark
rather than sinking -- a near-black chip inside a dark bubble reads as a hole, not as code.
#334's split, plus idle -- the state a room is created in (#489). This ramp is deliberately
independent of 'brand' so the
accent can change without re-teaching anyone what amber means. 'mark' and 'label' are not
decoration: roughly one man in twelve has some colour-vision deficiency and the phone case is
frequently bright sunlight, so a coloured dot alone is unreadable in both. Every surface that
renders a status must render its mark and its label, never the colour by itself.
'mark' names a SHAPE, not a character (#458). It was originally a literal codepoint, which
does not work: of the five originally chosen, three are absent from Source Sans 3 and one
from JetBrains Mono, and the two shipped faces share no checkmark and no cross at all -- so
no choice of characters can express this set. A codepoint a font lacks either renders as tofu
or falls back to whatever the device happens to have, which is the per-device resolution
decision 0006 exists to rule out, arriving on the one element the accessibility rule depends
on. Naming the shape instead lets each toolkit draw it natively: a StreamGeometry in
Aer.Ui/Theme/Icons.axaml keyed 'Icon.<Mark>', a CustomPainter in
Aer.Mobile/lib/theme/status_mark.dart. CI fails if either lacks a mark named here.
The shapes are chosen to differ in SILHOUETTE, because that is what the rule actually
requires -- marks that are only distinguishable once you can see their colour would pass
a naive reading of 'carries a glyph' and fail the people it is for. No two share an outline
at 16px in greyscale. Exception (#1132): queued is a step-level state and out-of-plan a
room-level one (verified: RoomCardStatus has no Queued member), so the two never render in the
same list; both are 'waiting, not asked to act', and desktop shipped this mark in #1116.
waitingToStart (#1296) is the same kind of exception: a room-level 'waiting, not asked to act'
state distinct from queued's step-level one, so the clock mark does not need to differ from
ellipsis in any way stronger than convention. Unlike every other status here, it is ephemeral --
an in-memory daemon fact, not something a journal predicate can produce -- and DeriveStatus
checks it first, ahead of every projection-derived arm; see decisions/0020's 2026-08-16
amendment.
'filled' states whether the shape is painted solid or stroked, and it lives here rather than
in each toolkit for a reason found the hard way (#461): the Avalonia call sites set Stroke and
never Fill, while the Flutter painter filled the same closed path, so one status rendered as an
outline on desktop and a solid on mobile. #458's gate cannot catch that -- it asserts a mark is
defined, not that the two drawings agree -- but fill is the part of 'agree' that can be made
declarative, so it is. Omitted means stroked.
idle is FILLED on purpose (#489). Icon.Dot is a closed circle and Icon.Ring is a 240-degree
arc, so stroked they differ only by a gap -- not a silhouette difference at 16px in
greyscale. A solid disc against an open arc is. Icon.Dot existed in Avalonia and in no
token before this: drawn on desktop, undrawable on mobile, and invisible to the gate,
because the check only walked token -> toolkit. It now walks both directions.
idle and the last three are quiet states and deliberately share one muted colour: you
are not being asked to act on, and giving each its own hue would spend the status ramp's
vocabulary on the states that matter least. They differ by mark, which is the channel that
carries meaning anyway.
'mark' is a plain shape-name string for every status but one. readyForReview's eye is the set's
first COMPOSITE mark -- a stroked lid with a filled pupil, two paint instructions in one shape
-- which the plain string can't express (#511): before this, Avalonia held both subpaths in one
StreamGeometry with one Fill/Stroke pair, so no value of 'filled' could stroke the lid and fill
the pupil, and setting either painted the whole almond solid or hollow. A composite mark's
'mark' is an ORDERED ARRAY of {geometry, filled} parts instead, painted in listed order; a plain
string is sugar for the single-part case. Each part's geometry name follows the same 'Icon.' +
Pascal-case convention as a plain mark, so the eye's parts are Icon.Eye (the lid, stroked) and
Icon.EyePupil (filled) -- both must exist in Icons.axaml, and the drift gate checks every part,
not just the first.
Decision 0058/#1318's scope ruling: the model tier as a mark, never the model string (0023
constraint 3 -- deep/balanced/fast). Drawn as an ascending three-dot meter, filled left to
right by tier. A SIBLING system to 'status' above, not a generalisation of it -- see the
'effort' block below for the shared reasoning on why fill count, not per-tier silhouette, is
the discriminator, and why the two meter families draw different shapes from each other and
from every status/vendor mark on the same chip.
Structurally wired ahead of its producer: nothing sets a worker's tier to one of these three
words yet -- #1330 owns measuring and registering the vendor-model -> tier mapping this block's
values will be read against. Until then the chip's own absence rule (ruling 2 on #1318) means
this mark renders nothing anywhere, which is expected and correct, not a bug to chase.
'steps' is the meter's total step count, read by both toolkits' hand-drawn meter geometry --
unlike 'mark' above this names no per-tier shape, because the shape at each position is the
SAME dot at every tier; only how many are filled changes. 'filled' is that count.
Decision 0058/#1318's scope ruling: how hard a worker thinks on this run, named by behaviour
(0023 -- quick/standard/careful/exhaustive) and drawn as an ascending four-bar meter, filled
left to right by tier. Wired live off docs/vendor-capabilities.md's canonical effort mapping
('The canonical effort mapping' section, the one register this value set is measured against);
the adapter (Aer.Adapters, never Aer.Flow/Aer.Ui/Aer.Mobile per 0023 constraint 1) is the only
place a vendor's raw effort string is known -- this block and the mark it draws never are.
Bars, not dots, and rectangular rather than round on purpose: 0058's own ruling on this record
(the #1318 scope ruling) names the discriminator as 'shape, fill or weight, never colour' for
these two meters, not full per-step silhouette distinctness the way 'status' above needs --  a
meter's FILL COUNT, read at its own family's step total, is exactly that. So 'balanced' (2 of 3
depth dots) is never mistaken for 'careful' (3 of 4 effort bars): the two families are drawn as
different shapes (round vs rectangular) precisely so a fill-count coincidence between them can
never read as the other family's tier, and neither collides with a status mark or a vendor mark
already on the same chip (0058 constraint 4).
'steps' and 'filled' mean exactly what they mean on 'depth' above -- see that block's own note.

spacing.$about: A scale, not a lookup of every gap in the gallery. Layout picks from these.

$about: Semantic roles rather than raw sizes, so a density switch changes one mapping instead of every
call site. Sizes here are the desktop ramp; 'density' scales the roles that differ on a phone.
fontFamily is RESOLVED (#453). Decision 0006 fixed the mechanism -- one variable font shipped as
an asset on both platforms, because Avalonia defaults to Segoe UI and Flutter to Roboto and a
family *name* resolves differently per device -- and left the face open; the owner chose Source
Sans 3 for prose and JetBrains Mono for code, reviewed as rendered specimens in these components.
These names are only safe because the matching files ship in-repo -- src/Aer.Ui/Assets/Fonts and
src/Aer.Mobile/assets/fonts. Never point these at a family that is not shipped alongside: that
is precisely the per-device resolution 0006 rules out.
Why this pairing and not Source's own matched mono: Source Code Pro is drawn from the same
skeleton as Source Sans, so code blended into prose. A mono built for reading code separates the
two on sight while staying calm beside a humanist sans.
Two densities over the same tokens, not a second design. Desktop is a workstation surface --
compact rows, more visible at once, pointer targets. Mobile is a glance surface -- taller rows,
real tap targets, larger type.
PROVISIONAL. Decision 0006 explicitly does not settle motion -- it belongs with the switcher
build (#336). These exist so the switcher has named slots to fill rather than ad-hoc durations
scattering through two toolkits before anyone decides. Expect them to be replaced, not extended.
